I've shared a desk with Nilesh through three years of engineering, and I've never seen him as angry as when Rishi left our course to join a music college. "Irresponsible. Selfish. His parents paid for this," Nilesh said, so loudly that the canteen went quiet. He kept going for days, forwarding the group articles about struggling musicians. It seemed like a lot for someone who barely knew Rishi.
Then last Sunday I dropped by his hostel room to return a charger. There was a guitar under his bed, with new strings, and a notebook of chord charts in his handwriting. He pushed it further under with his foot and said, "My cousin's."
I'm Gurleen, not a mind reader, so I don't know what's going on in his head. But I noticed the chords were for the same songs he says he hates.

qa.a: A guitar with new strings and a notebook of chord charts in his handwriting.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do next without accusing Nilesh?
qa.a: Say something light and open, like 'Your cousin has good taste in strings', and leave room for Nilesh to talk about music if he ever wants to.

qa.q: How might Rishi feel if he heard what was said in the canteen?
qa.a: Hurt and judged by someone who barely knew him, and perhaps confused later if he learned that Nilesh plays too.

grounding: A classmate notices that a student's furious scorn for a friend who chose music is far bigger than the situation, then glimpses his own hidden guitar.

Week one. When Alka posted photos from the college fest's dance night, Bhupen called them "shameless" in the class group. Then he messaged her privately, a long paragraph about wasted time and cheap music. Alka, puzzled, replied, "It was just dancing?"
Week two. Bhupen skipped the next dance night but walked past the hall twice. Later his roommate heard him in the bathroom, humming the fest song very softly.
Week four. Alka found him standing outside the hall again. "You can come in, you know," she said. He started to snap about shameless people, then stopped. His hands were in his pockets. "I don't know how," he said. "I've never danced. I always wanted to."
Alka held the door open and waited.

qa.q: What did Bhupen call the dance-night photos in the class group?
qa.a: Shameless.

qa.q: Why was Bhupen's reaction to a few dance photos so fierce?
qa.a: Bhupen felt embarrassed about secretly wanting to dance without knowing how, and condemning it loudly kept that longing hidden, even from himself.

qa.q: What turning point came in week four, and what made it possible?
qa.a: Bhupen stopped mid-snap and admitted he had always wanted to dance; Alka's easy invitation, with no teasing, made that feel safe.

qa.q: How did Alka experience Bhupen's long private message in week one?
qa.a: She was puzzled, because his heat didn't match something as ordinary as dancing, as her reply 'It was just dancing?' shows.

grounding: Over four weeks a student who condemns dance nights with unusual heat is revealed to be drawn to dancing himself.

When I was twenty, in Indore, my friend Ashok announced he was taking a year off to travel the Himalayas by bus. I was furious. I told everyone he was a loafer, that his father's hard-earned money was being wasted, that travellers were just people running from responsibility. I went on about it for months, far more than anyone needed. Finally your Nani asked me, "Vijay, why do you keep talking about Ashok's trip?" I had no answer. That night I took out the map I'd hidden inside my accounts textbook, with routes marked in pencil. I had been planning that same trip for years and was too scared to go. The anger was about me, beta, not Ashok. So go, and send me photos.

qa.q: Where had Vijay hidden his map?
qa.a: Inside his accounts textbook, with routes marked in pencil.

qa.q: Why did Vijay's anger at Ashok last for months?
qa.a: Ashok was doing the very trip Vijay secretly longed for and feared; condemning it kept his own wish buried.

qa.q: What turning point helped Vijay see the truth?
qa.a: Nani's simple question about why he kept talking about Ashok's trip, which sent him back to the hidden map.

qa.q: How might Ashok have felt hearing he was called a loafer?
qa.a: Probably hurt and confused, since his friend's anger was much bigger than a travel plan deserved.

grounding: An uncle tells how, at twenty, he condemned a friend's travel year with far too much heat because he secretly longed to make the same trip.

Placement week had the whole hostel on edge, and Arohi's first interview was at two. In the crowded mess at noon, Kamal said casually that he'd skip placements and spend a year on an organic farm in Himachal.
Arohi put her spoon down. "That's so irresponsible. It's a fantasy for people with safety nets. You'll be back in three months, broke, calling it 'a journey'." She kept going, louder, until the next table turned round.
Kamal blinked. "It's one year, Arohi. Why are you so angry?"
She didn't answer. Back in her room, with forty minutes left, she opened her laptop to revise. Instead her cursor drifted to a bookmarks folder named "someday": farm stays, volunteer listings, a village school in Spiti. She had been adding to it for two years. She shut the laptop hard and picked up her formal shoes.

qa.q: What was in Arohi's bookmarks folder named "someday"?
qa.a: Farm stays, volunteer listings and a village school in Spiti.

qa.q: Why might attacking Kamal's plan feel justified to Arohi in the moment?
qa.a: Attacking Kamal's plan protects Arohi from feeling torn; if the farm year is only a fantasy, the pull she feels toward it, two years of bookmarks, doesn't have to be faced.

qa.q: What could Arohi do with Kamal's question, "Why are you so angry?"
qa.a: Treat it as a clue rather than an insult, and ask herself honestly what the farm year stirred up, maybe even telling Kamal about her own folder later.

qa.q: How might Kamal see Arohi's outburst in the mess?
qa.a: Kamal seems surprised and puzzled that a casual plan drew such a loud attack, and may feel judged for something that isn't really about Kamal at all.

grounding: Shows a young adult who condemns a friend's farm year with heat out of proportion to the situation, while privately drawn to the same life.

In their rented room in Salt Lake, Payal was ironing a kurta for Saturday's open-mic poetry night. "Come with me, Indu. Just to listen."
Indu didn't look up from her accounting textbook. "Please. Standing up and reading your diary to strangers? It's so self-obsessed. Everyone snapping their fingers like it's deep." Her voice sharpened. "Honestly, it's embarrassing, Payal. Grown people fishing for claps."
Payal set the iron down. "That was a lot. I only asked if you wanted to come."
"I'm just being honest."
After Payal left, Indu sat very still. Then she slid a thin blue notebook out from under her mattress. Its pages were full of short lines about her grandmother's kitchen, the metro at night, the ache of leaving home. She read one under her breath, the way people did on stage, and quickly shut it.

qa.q: Where did Indu keep the thin blue notebook?
qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: Why might sneering at the open mic feel reasonable to Indu?
qa.a: Calling it self-obsessed keeps her own wish to share her poems safely hidden; if reading on stage is embarrassing, she never has to risk it.

qa.q: What choice is open to Indu after she reads a poem under her breath?
qa.a: She could admit to herself, and maybe to Payal, that part of her wants to go, and try simply listening at one open mic.

qa.q: What might Payal take away from saying "That was a lot"?
qa.a: Payal noticed the reply was far harsher than a simple invitation deserved, and may feel stung and puzzled about why Indu cares so much.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who scorns open-mic poetry with unusual heat while secretly writing poems, the intensity pointing to the opposite pull.
